common_name: Jackson Pecan (Scab-Tolerant Mississippi Gulf Coast Pecan, Type I)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Jackson is a Type I (protandrous) pecan, so pair it with a Type II cultivar such as Stuart or Elliott for reliable cross-pollination and a heavier nut set.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving it room to grow into a large shade tree and siting a Type II pollinator nearby since pecans are wind-pollinated and set fruit far more reliably with a cross-pollinator present. Jackson traces to an early-1900s open-pollinated seedling selection from Ocean Springs on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, the same coastal nursery district that produced Stuart, Schley, and Forkert, and it carries the moderate scab tolerance typical of that old Gulf Coast selection group, making it a more forgiving choice than scab-susceptible standards like Burkett in Louisiana and Mississippi's humid summers. Nuts run 33-38 per pound with a good 52-56% kernel percentage and solid classic pecan flavor. Water deeply through nut fill in late summer and apply a foliar zinc spray each spring, since pecans are notoriously heavy zinc feeders on Gulf Coast soils.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Select Scab-Resistant Pecan Varieties for Home Orchards
Mississippi State University Extension — Fruit and Nut Review: Pecans in the Home Landscape
University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program — Cultivar Notes

common_name: Syrup Mill Pecan (Exceptionally Scab-Resistant Alabama Gulf Coast Pecan)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Syrup Mill is a Type I (protandrous) pecan noted as a good pollinator for Type II cultivars such as Elliott and Kanza.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and pair with a compatible Type II cultivar for cross-pollination; Syrup Mill was found in Mobile County on the Alabama Gulf Coast and has shown even higher resistance to pecan scab than the long-standard Elliott in university disease trials, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for humid coastal home orchards. The tree is notably vigorous and holds clean, healthy foliage through the growing season, which supports steadier nut fill in wet years when scab-prone cultivars are already defoliating. Nuts run smaller than many named cultivars, around 65 per pound, with roughly 47% kernel, so it suits growers who prioritize dependable low-input production and disease resistance over maximum nut size. Trees begin bearing within about seven years of planting; water deeply during nut fill and correct zinc deficiency with an annual spring foliar spray.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Select Scab-Resistant Pecan Varieties for Home Orchards
University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program — Review of Scab-Resistant Cultivars
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Pecan Cultivar Recommendations

common_name: Avalon Pecan (Modern UGA Scab-Resistant Large-Nut Pecan, Type II)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Avalon is a Type II (protogynous) pecan, so pair it with a Type I cultivar such as Cape Fear, Gafford, or Desirable for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible Type I pollinator nearby for a good nut set. Avalon is a modern cultivar released by the University of Georgia pecan breeding program in Tifton, carrying the scab-resistant Gloria Grande in its parentage, and it combines large, high-quality nuts with disease resistance that university scab trials have found superior to most other cultivars of similar size — a rare pairing, since many large-nut pecans are scab-prone. Nuts run 46-54 per pound with a strong 53-54% kernel percentage, and the tree bears precociously, reaching far heavier yields by its sixth to eighth year than older standards like Desirable. Because it is a recent release, Avalon has a shorter Gulf South track record than heirloom cultivars, but its combination of size, quality, and scab resistance makes it a promising choice for home orchards willing to plant a newer variety. Water deeply through nut fill and apply a spring foliar zinc spray as with any pecan.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program — Avalon Cultivar Profile
HortScience — 'Avalon', a New Pecan Cultivar with High Levels of Resistance to Pecan Scab (2018)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pecan Variety Selection

common_name: Woodman Pecan (Low-Input Scab-Resistant South Louisiana Pecan)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted trees in late winter into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Woodman is a good Type I pollinator for Type II cultivars such as Elliott and Kanza.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and pair with a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Kanza for cross-pollination. Woodman originated in south Louisiana, where it was identified by grower Hilary Langlois on land once owned by his uncle, and it has earned a following among LSU AgCenter-recommended cultivars for outstanding resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that limits pecan production across the humid Gulf Coast. The tree is notably vigorous and productive even under low-input management, bearing a crop most years with minimal fertilizer or spray, which makes it a practical choice for home orchardists who do not want to run an intensive spray program. Because it is a relatively new introduction from a single grower's selection rather than a formally released breeding-program cultivar, published nut-size and kernel-percentage data are limited; growers should expect the vigorous growth and disease resistance typical of other South Louisiana scab-resistant selections. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer and correct zinc deficiency with an annual spring foliar spray.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — From Tree to Table: A Guide to Growing Disease-Resistant Pecan Varieties in Louisiana
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Growing Pecan Trees: A Guide to a Fruitful Investment
